claims.text: The equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The full Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The full Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has stronger solute-dislocation interactions than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Local distortion fields alter the activation energy for slip.
Local distortion fields alter the activation energy for cross-slip.
Changes in slip and cross-slip activation produce differences in work hardening and failure behavior despite a common FCC phase structure.
Local lattice distortion and chemical complexity mediate dislocation pinning and slip-system activation.
The presence of all five elements produces a broader distribution of atomic sizes and bonding characteristics than occurs in the quaternary and ternary subsets.
A broader distribution of atomic sizes and bonding characteristics increases local lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion enhances solute-dislocation pinning.
Enhanced solute-dislocation pinning raises the work-hardening rate and delays necking.
Removing one or more elements reduces the magnitude and diversity of local lattice distortions.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower work-hardening rates under the same deformation conditions.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower ductility and undergo earlier necking and failure.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less pronounced lattice-distortion fields than the quinary alloy.

The proposed relationships apply when all alloys remain single-phase FCC, receive identical processing, and are deformed at room temperature at moderate strain rates without phase transformation or appreciable adiabatic heating.
